Comments on Ross Ice Shelf Project Draft Environmental Impact Statement
1. While the probability of a well blowout from drilling to a depth of 150-200 m is perhaps extremely remote, the advisability of drilling blindly with no knowledge of the geophysical conditions remains very questionable. A seismic survey should be conducted despite the cost. The information obtained should be of great value to the Ross Ice Shelf Project and should remove the risk involved with drilling blindly. To do otherwise would not be prudent.
2. Based on information obtained from controlled spills under ice (Glaeser and Vance 1971) and theoretical studies (Wolfe and Hoult 1972) any oil released by a blowout would be expected to be trapped in depressions on the underside of the ice. This oil may be frozen into the underside of the ice depending on the ice growth and heat transfer situation. Assuming the oil is not frozen into the ice, adhesion to the under ice surface and a lack of current will prevent the oil from flowing up the gentle slope of the Ross Ice Shelf to the sea. Without biodegradation it would take 1,000 years for this oil to reach the Ross Sea. Additional information on the behavior of oil spilled under sea ice is expected to be obtained from the Canadian Beaufort Sea Project now taking place.
3. As a result of field work in the Arctic Ocean and laboratory investigations (Button 1974) biodegradation can be expected to occur provided the oil has not frozen into the underside of the ice. The lighter crude oil fractions will probably be degraded in less than a month. The higher fractions, due to a lack of turbulence, may have a residence time on the order of ten years.
4. The cleanup of an oil spill under Arctic Pack Ice, 3 meters thick, would, at present, be an extremely difficult task. The cleanup of a spill under 300-500 meters of ice would be impossible.
References
Button, D. K., <u>Arctic Oil Biodegradation</u>, Office of Research and Development, U.S. Coast Guard, Unpublished Manuscript 1974. (Expected Publication Date - January 1975.)
Glaeser, John L. and Vance, George, P., A Study of the Behavior of Oil Spills in the Arctic, Office of Research and Development, U.S. Coast Guard, February 1971.
Wolfe, L. S. and Hoult, David P., <u>Effects of Oil Under Sea Ice</u>, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Department of Mechanical Engineering, August 1972.
